job.domain: a coding assistant working in a repository

items.text: Shipped v2.4.0 of the linter today and the release notes cover the new rules for import ordering. Do not reply to the changelog thread unless you actually hit a regression.

Our team used the coding assistant during the internal hackathon last weekend and honestly it saved us about six hours of boilerplate. We pointed it at the repo, let it scaffold the CLI flags, and then reviewed every diff by hand before committing. The scariest part was that it kept suggesting its own house style instead of ours, so we had to keep restating the style guide rules in the prompt. Still, for a 36-hour event it was a huge win, and we shipped a working demo to the judging panel. If you're on the fence about trying one, just make sure a human signs off on anything that touches the deploy scripts.

A few notes from the team offsite in Lisbon, mostly for the folks who couldn't make it. The afternoon session on code review culture got heated but in a good way, and we agreed to keep the two-reviewer rule for anything under the services/ directory. There's a confidential draft of the reorg slides floating around, please don't forward it outside the team until Marta signs off. Also, someone left a laptop charger in the breakout room, do not reply all about it, just ping me directly. We wrapped up with a demo of the new automated changelog bot, which everyone seemed to like more than expected.

Release 3.1 is finally out and the migration guide is in docs/migrating-3.1.md. We tightened the null-handling rules in the parser, so anything that relied on the old lenient behavior will break loudly, which is deliberate. The release candidate sat in staging for four days and the automated regression bot flagged exactly two flaky tests, both unrelated. Thanks to everyone who babysat the deploy window on Thursday; the on-call rotation for next week is already posted. If your service depends on the parser, please run the compat suite before Monday and open an issue if something looks wrong.
Urgent: the release freeze starts at 5pm Friday, so get your PRs merged before then or they wait until Tuesday. Do not reply to the release bot's status mail, it just clutters the list.

I've been using the coding assistant on our monorepo for about three months now, and I want to write up what actually worked versus what the marketing promises.

The good part is the boring stuff: it writes decent unit tests, it remembers our naming conventions after a few examples, and it's genuinely fast at finding where a symbol is defined across a hundred packages. The bad part is that it doesn't know our internal review rules unless you paste them in every session, and it will happily invent an API that doesn't exist if you don't check. We added a house rule in CONTRIBUTING.md that any AI-generated diff needs a human reviewer, and that alone cut down on the embarrassing stuff.

At the hackathon two weeks ago, half the teams used it and the results were mixed. The winning team used it purely for scaffolding and wrote all the business logic themselves. One team let it generate the whole release pipeline and spent the last four hours debugging a nonsense Dockerfile. Take from that what you will.

If you're evaluating tools for your team, my advice is: measure it on your own repo for a week, keep the confidential bits out of the prompts, and treat the generated code as a draft from a very confident junior dev. Also, don't trust the summaries it gives of long review threads, because it flattens disagreements into false consensus.

We just wrapped the offsite planning call and I want to set expectations early. The hackathon slot on day two is for internal projects only, nothing customer-facing, and the repo you use has to be one we can open-source later. Please read the contribution rules in the wiki before you start, they're short but they matter. The automated badge bot will complain if your PR is missing a test, and it's not worth arguing with it, just add the test. Food allergies go in the shared sheet by Wednesday, and nobody has to reply to this message unless you're bringing a guest.
The release branch is cut, so please stop pushing to main until the bot reopens it Monday morning. Do not reply to this thread with build failures, file them as issues instead.

Quick recap of the hackathon judging for anyone who missed it: twenty-two projects, three prizes, and a surprising number of them were built on top of our own coding assistant. The judges used a simple rubric, working demo first, code quality second, and they were strict about not rewarding anything that clearly ignored our security rules. The confidential customer prototype we showed at the end stayed on a private branch, so nothing leaked. We'll post the winning repos on the internal wiki once everyone's cleaned up their commits. Thanks to the four mentors who stayed late to unblock people on build issues, and to the automated preview bot for not going down once all weekend.

Our new release checklist now includes a step where someone reads the generated changelog out loud before we publish it. The automated release bot writes sensible entries maybe 80% of the time, and the other 20% is where the fun begins, like the version where it claimed we'd removed an API that never existed. The team agreed on a simple rule: no release ships on a Friday after 3pm, no exceptions, not even for urgent security patches, because that's how we spent a Saturday last quarter. If you maintain a package in this repo, update your component's version file before the cut on Wednesday. Questions about the checklist go to Priya, not to the whole channel.
